reference.source: Standard gynaecology textbook and vulval surgery guidance
clinicalPearls: A Bartholin cyst forms when the duct of a greater vestibular gland becomes obstructed and mucus accumulates, producing a soft, usually painless swelling at the posterior part of the labium majus (classically the four- and eight-o'clock positions)
An uninfected cyst is often an incidental finding, whereas secondary infection produces a tender, hot, fluctuant abscess with surrounding oedema and difficulty sitting or walking
The key clinical distinction is the quiescent obstructed-duct cyst versus an acutely inflamed Bartholin abscess, which changes management from observation to drainage
Small asymptomatic cysts in younger women can simply be observed, sometimes with warm baths to encourage spontaneous drainage
Symptomatic cysts and abscesses are treated by drainage with a technique that creates a lasting epithelialised tract, such as marsupialisation or insertion of a Word catheter, to reduce recurrence
Simple incision and drainage alone tends to recur because the duct opening reseals, so a fistulising procedure is preferred
Antibiotics are reserved for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, or high-risk patients rather than for uncomplicated drainage
A new or solid Bartholin-area mass in a woman over the age of about forty, or an atypical or recurrent lesion, warrants biopsy to exclude the rare Bartholin gland carcinoma
reference.pathophysiology: The greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands lie deep to the posterior vulva and secrete mucus through ducts opening into the vestibule to lubricate the introitus. When a duct becomes obstructed, often after inflammation or minor trauma, secretions are retained and the duct distends into a cyst. If the retained fluid becomes secondarily infected, typically by mixed vaginal and enteric organisms, an abscess develops with the classic features of acute inflammation. Because the underlying problem is a blocked duct, treatments that merely evacuate the contents without maintaining an open drainage tract allow re-obstruction and recurrence.
additionalDifferentials: Vulval sebaceous or epidermoid inclusion cyst
Cyst of the canal of Nuck (hydrocele)
Vaginal wall cyst (e.g. Gartner duct cyst)
Bartholin gland carcinoma or other vulval malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Clinical inspection and palpation to characterise the swelling and detect fluctuance
Swab of any purulent discharge for culture, including screening for sexually transmitted infection where relevant
Biopsy or excision histology of solid, atypical, or recurrent lesions to exclude malignancy
Pelvic or vulval ultrasound if the anatomy or diagnosis is uncertain
Assessment for diabetes or immunosuppression in recurrent abscesses
redFlags: A solid or irregular Bartholin-area mass, particularly in a woman over forty, raising concern for carcinoma
Rapidly spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or features suggesting necrotising infection
Recurrent abscesses that may indicate underlying diabetes or immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: Most Bartholin cysts and abscesses resolve well after drainage with a fistulising technique, though recurrence can occur; the rare Bartholin gland carcinoma carries a far more serious prognosis and must not be missed in older women.
pitfalls: Performing simple incision and drainage without a marsupialisation or catheter technique, leading to recurrence
Missing a Bartholin gland carcinoma by assuming any posterior vulval mass in an older woman is a benign cyst
Prescribing antibiotics for a fluctuant abscess instead of draining it
Failing to consider diabetes or immunosuppression in recurrent disease
Mistaking other vulval or vaginal cysts for a Bartholin cyst because of location
references: Standard gynaecology reference text on vulval and vaginal cysts
Vulval surgery and minor procedures guidance
management: Observation of small asymptomatic cysts, with warm sitz baths to encourage spontaneous drainage
Marsupialisation or Word catheter insertion for symptomatic cysts to create a lasting drainage tract
Avoidance of simple incision and drainage alone, which tends to recur as the duct reseals
Swab and treatment of any secondary infection, screening for sexually transmitted organisms where relevant
Gland excision for recurrent cysts resistant to fistulising procedures
Biopsy or excision histology of solid, atypical or recurrent lesions, particularly in older women, to exclude Bartholin gland carcinoma
Assessment for diabetes or immunosuppression in recurrent disease
